source.title: Random Initialization Can't Catch Up: The Advantage of Language Model Transfer for Time Series Forecasting
source.authors: Roland Riachi; Kashif Rasul; Arjun Ashok; Prateek Humane; Alexis Roger; A. Williams; Yuriy Nevmyvaka; Irina Rish

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or garbling. Figure plots are not numerically readable in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: Tests downstream validation-loss trends with model scale in time-series forecasting, a new setting, but does not fit or test the original language-model scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports time-series validation-loss curves for different initializations, tokenizers and backbone sizes. Only the backbone-size comparison bears on V6. It does not fit power laws, test extrapolation from small runs, or find a compute-optimal parameter/token split. Cited results and hyperparameter choices are not recorded as result rows.
record.test_reason: Compares time-series validation loss across three T5 sizes (60M/220M/770M), with language-pretrained and random initialization. This bears on whether downstream loss improves with pretrained scale (V6) and whether loss falls with size in a new modality trained from scratch (V5). No power laws are fitted.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Language-pretrained initialization beats random initialization across tokenizers, sizes and post-training. Larger pretrained models help most in the low-data regime, and Flan-T5 underperforms T5. Add: a non-vanishing transfer gap persists because random-init models plateau, contrary to Hernandez et al. (2021).
record.recipe_differences: The study fine-tunes T5 backbones for univariate time-series forecasting and compares initialization, tokenization and backbone size. It does not use the original text-pretraining loss measurement, fit scaling laws, extrapolate runs or optimize a compute budget.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that initialization, tokenizer and backbone size affect validation loss; its hyperparameter sweep also reports differences across learning rate, batch size, weight decay and warm-up settings.

fits_no_version.finding: The transfer gap between language-initialized and random-initialized models does not vanish with more time-series tokens. This contrasts with Hernandez et al. (2021) scaling laws for transfer; effective data transferred has vertical asymptotes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Effective data transferred from language pretraining follows a predictable law that vanishes with ample target data (Hernandez et al. 2021 transfer scaling).

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says trained checkpoints and code will be released upon acceptance
record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267 (2025)
record.problems: The scale comparison is limited to the T5 family and three model sizes. The relevant Figure 3 results are not numerically readable in the supplied text, and no power-law fit or uncertainty estimate for that comparison is reported.
record.rows_left_out: Figures 1–2 and 5–7 report initialization, tokenizer and effective-transfer comparisons, but do not test the downstream scale-predictability result in V6 or fit a power law. Figure 8 reports mean and standard deviations across hyperparameter configurations, not a scaling-law result.

untested.parts: No text-pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No power-law form is fitted for time-series training or transfer; only the direction of the size effect is reported.
Downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss; tasks other than univariate forecasting; models beyond T5; predictability (no fitted trend).
No exponents or fitting choices compared.

missing.what: Effective transfer across backbone scales; the authors state that scaling parameter count increases effective transfer. Also the random-minus-language loss difference across scales.

record.verdict_notes: All scale evidence is figure-only, with three sizes of one model family and no power-law fits. The V6 link rests on treating time-series fine-tuning loss as downstream performance of a language-pretrained model. The V5 link for R3 treats from-scratch time-series training as a new modality. Hyperparameters were tuned only at 220M, which may confound the size comparisons.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law loss versus parameters, tokens or compute in language-model pretraining.
No small-run fits or predictions of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute budget comparison or compute-optimal allocation of parameters and tokens.
No comparison of depth, width or other architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
The paper studies time-series forecasting and transfer, but does not test whether a power-law form holds in that setting; no power-law fits are reported.
Tests model-scale trends on one time-series forecasting setup, but not downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss or across other tasks.
No fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits are compared across fitting choices.

rows.subject: T5 backbones initialized with language weights (small, base and large)
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation loss across backbone sizes during time-series training.
rows.note: The authors state that larger pre-trained models outperform smaller ones in the low-data regime. This is a reported aggregate trend across the three sizes; individual numeric losses are not given in the supplied text.
rows.check: Direction only: larger pretrained models have lower loss in the low-data regime. Figure-only, with no numbers or fit.

rows.subject: T5 backbones initialized with language weights (small, base and large)
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation loss across backbone sizes as time-series training continued.
rows.measure: Validation loss and difference between model sizes
rows.note: The authors say the differences between model sizes taper as training continues; the pre-trained models had not converged within the tested training duration.
rows.check: Authors say the size differences taper as training continues. Pretrained models had not converged within the training length, so the end-of-training size ordering cannot be read from the text.

rows.subject: Randomly initialized T5 backbones (small, base and large)
rows.stage_stated: trained on time-series data from random initialization
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation loss across backbone sizes during time-series training.
rows.note: The authors describe an inverse relationship between scale and validation loss for randomly initialized models: larger models have worse validation loss, and these models converge earlier.
rows.check: Randomly initialized models get no language pretraining, so this is not a downstream-from-pretraining result for V6. It is from-scratch training in a new modality (time series), so it bears on V5. Authors state an inverse relation between scale and validation loss. Figure-only, no fit, and hyperparameters were swept only at 220M.

relationships.condition: Language-pretrained T5 backbones, low-data regime of time-series fine-tuning
relationships.reason: Larger pretrained backbones give lower downstream validation loss early in training (R1); direction only, figure-based.
relationships.display_finding: Larger language-pretrained backbones achieved lower downstream validation loss early in training, establishing an improvement trend.

relationships.condition: Language-pretrained T5 backbones, later in time-series training
relationships.reason: The scale advantage tapers as fine-tuning data grows (R2), so the gain from scale depends on the amount of downstream data.
relationships.display_finding: The advantage of larger backbones tapered as downstream fine-tuning data increased.

relationships.condition: Randomly initialized T5 trained from scratch on time series (LOTSA)
relationships.reason: Larger models reach worse validation loss and plateau early (R3). Whether data or hyperparameters (tuned only at 220M) are the bottleneck is unclear, so this qualifies rather than refutes V5.
relationships.display_finding: Larger models reached worse validation loss and plateaued early, with data constraints and hyperparameters tuned only at 220M remaining possible bottlenecks.
